summary: Psalm 96 calls the whole earth to sing to Yahweh, announce his salvation, and declare his glory among the nations. It contrasts Yahweh, maker of the heavens, with the idols of the peoples, then summons nations, worshipers, and creation itself to rejoice because Yahweh reigns and comes to judge rightly.
whyItMatters: Within Book IV of Psalms, this chapter places security and praise in Yahweh’s kingship rather than in a human ruler. It shows praise expanding outward: Israel’s song becomes an announcement to the nations and even to the heavens, earth, sea, fields, and trees.

context.author: No individual author is named in the chapter. Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections, and authorship for individual psalms is often uncertain.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving these words for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; the five-book Psalter is a later anthology, so one date for the whole book would be misleading.
context.setting: Psalm 96 belongs in Book IV of Psalms, a section that emphasizes Yahweh’s reign, creation, and enduring rule. The chapter itself imagines worship in Yahweh’s courts and praise announced among all nations.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and public praise, built through repeated commands, parallel lines, and widening summonses to the earth, nations, and creation.

outline.heading: A New Song for All the Earth
outline.note: The psalm opens with repeated calls to sing, bless, proclaim, and declare Yahweh’s salvation and glory among all peoples.

outline.heading: Yahweh Above the Idols
outline.note: The reason for praise is given: Yahweh is great, the maker of the heavens, and honor, majesty, strength, and beauty belong before him.

outline.heading: The Nations Summoned to Worship
outline.note: Families of nations are told to ascribe glory and strength to Yahweh, bring an offering, enter his courts, worship, and tremble before him.

outline.heading: Yahweh Reigns and Judges
outline.note: The nations are to hear that Yahweh reigns, the world is established, and he will judge the peoples with equity.

outline.heading: Creation Rejoices Before the Judge
outline.note: Heavens, earth, sea, field, and trees are invited into joy because Yahweh comes to judge the world with righteousness and truth.

keyVerses.text: Sing to Yahweh a new song! Sing to Yahweh, all the earth.
keyVerses.why: This opening line sets the chapter’s tone: praise is not limited to one group but is addressed to all the earth.

keyVerses.text: For all the gods of the peoples are idols, but Yahweh made the heavens.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter’s central contrast between the idols of the peoples and Yahweh as creator.

keyVerses.text: Say among the nations, “Yahweh reigns.” The world is also established. It can’t be moved. He will judge the peoples with equity.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s public announcement: Yahweh’s reign is to be declared among the nations and is linked with stable, fair judgment.

keyVerses.text: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.
keyVerses.why: The final verse explains why creation rejoices: Yahweh’s coming judgment is described as righteous and true.

themes: A new song for all the earth

questions.question: Who is being told to sing in this psalm?
questions.answer: The command is broader than one choir or one nation. Verse 1 says, “all the earth,” and verses 3, 7, and 10 bring the nations and peoples into view. The chapter imagines Yahweh’s praise being announced beyond Israel’s own worshiping community.

questions.question: What is a “new song”?
questions.answer: The chapter does not explain the phrase as a technical category. In this psalm, the “new song” is connected with fresh public praise: singing, blessing Yahweh’s name, proclaiming his salvation, and declaring his glory among the nations.

questions.question: What does the psalm mean by “salvation” here?
questions.answer: Verse 2 tells worshipers to proclaim Yahweh’s salvation “from day to day,” but it does not narrate one specific rescue event. In the chapter, salvation is part of the public message about Yahweh’s greatness, glory, and reign.

questions.question: Why does the psalm compare Yahweh with other gods?
questions.answer: Verses 4-5 give a reason for Yahweh to be praised and feared above all gods. The contrast is blunt: “all the gods of the peoples are idols,” while Yahweh “made the heavens.” The chapter’s claim rests on Yahweh as creator, not on a debate narrated in detail.

questions.question: What are “courts” in verse 8?
questions.answer: The chapter speaks in worship language: bringing an offering and coming into Yahweh’s courts. It points to a sacred worship setting without pausing to describe its architecture. In Psalms more broadly, many poems are oriented toward Jerusalem and temple worship, but this verse itself simply uses the language of entering Yahweh’s courts.

questions.question: Does “tremble before him” mean terror only?
questions.answer: Verse 9 pairs worship with trembling before Yahweh, and verse 4 says he is “to be feared above all gods.” The chapter presents this fear as reverent awe before the great creator and judge. It is not described as panic over moral guilt in this psalm.

questions.question: Why is judgment a reason for joy?
questions.answer: That can sound strange to many readers because judgment is often heard only as threat. In Psalm 96, creation rejoices because Yahweh’s judgment is described with “equity,” “righteousness,” and “truth.” The psalm presents judgment as the world being rightly governed by Yahweh.

questions.question: Are the heavens, sea, fields, and trees literally praising?
questions.answer: The psalm uses poetic summons: heavens are glad, earth rejoices, the sea roars, fields exult, and trees sing for joy. Readers differ on how literally to describe creation’s participation, but the chapter clearly presents the created world as involved in the joy of Yahweh’s coming rule.

questions.question: How have later readers connected this psalm with wider mission or messianic hope?
questions.answer: The chapter itself commands Yahweh’s glory and reign to be declared among the nations. Later Jewish and Christian readers have often heard that worldwide scope in relation to their own hopes and worship. Those later uses should be kept distinct from the chapter’s own immediate speech, which is a summons to praise Yahweh as creator, king, and judge.

glossary.def: The divine name used throughout this translation of the psalm. The chapter addresses Yahweh as creator, king, and judge.
The word used in verse 5 for the gods of the peoples, set in contrast with Yahweh who made the heavens.
Something brought in worship. In verse 8 it belongs with coming into Yahweh’s courts and giving glory due to his name.
The quality named in verse 10 for Yahweh’s judgment of the peoples; in this chapter it signals fair and right rule.
